title: Networking & Communication Protocols
summary: Complete networking guide — OSI/TCP-IP layers, DNS resolution, TCP vs UDP internals, HTTP evolution, REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL, WebSockets, and protocol selection for system design.

explanation.overview:
Every system design involves components communicating over a network. Understanding protocols — their strengths, weaknesses, and internals — lets you make informed choices about how services talk to each other. This chapter covers everything from low-level TCP to high-level API paradigms. DEVELOPER BLOG INSIGHT: 'There is no perfect protocol; every choice is a trade-off between latency, throughput, complexity, and payload size.' ## Domain name system


Source: DNS security presentation

A Domain Name System (DNS) translates a domain name such as www.example.com to an IP address. DNS is hierarchical, with a few authoritative servers at the top level. Your router or ISP provides information about which DNS server(s) to contact when doing a lookup. Lower level DNS servers cache mappings, which could become stale due to DNS propagation delays. DNS results can also be cached by your browser or OS for a certain period of time, determined by the [time to live (TTL)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_to_live). * **NS record (name server)** - Specifies the DNS servers for your domain/subdomain. * **MX record (mail exchange)** - Specifies the mail servers for accepting messages. * **A record (address)** - Points a name to an IP address. * **CNAME (canonical)** - Points a name to another name or `CNAME` (example.com to www.example.com) or to an `A` record. Services such as [CloudFlare](https://www.cloudflare.com/dns/) and [Route 53](https://aws.amazon.com/route53/) provide managed DNS services. Some DNS services can route traffic through various methods: * [Weighted round robin](https://www.jscape.com/blog/load-balancing-algorithms) * Prevent traffic from going to servers under maintenance * Balance between varying cluster sizes * A/B testing * [Latency-based](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/routing-policy-latency.html) * [Geolocation-based](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/routing-policy-geo.html) ### Disadvantage(s): DNS * Accessing a DNS server introduces a slight delay, although mitigated by caching described above. * DNS server management could be complex and is generally managed by [governments, ISPs, and large companies](http://superuser.com/questions/472695/who-controls-the-dns-servers/472729). * DNS services have recently come under [DDoS attack](http://dyn.com/blog/dyn-analysis-summary-of-friday-october-21-attack/), preventing users from accessing websites such as Twitter without knowing Twitter's IP address(es). ### Source(s) and further reading * [DNS architecture](https://technet.microsoft.com/en-us/library/dd197427(v=ws.10).aspx) * [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_Name_System) * [DNS articles](https://support.dnsimple.com/categories/dns/) ## Communication


Source: OSI 7 layer model

### Hypertext transfer protocol (HTTP) HTTP is a method for encoding and transporting data between a client and a server. It is a request/response protocol: clients issue requests and servers issue responses with relevant content and completion status info about the request. HTTP is self-contained, allowing requests and responses to flow through many intermediate routers and servers that perform load balancing, caching, encryption, and compression. A basic HTTP request consists of a verb (method) and a resource (endpoint). Below are common HTTP verbs: | Verb | Description | Idempotent* | Safe | Cacheable | |---|---|---|---|---| | GET | Reads a resource | Yes | Yes | Yes | | POST | Creates a resource or trigger a process that handles data | No | No | Yes if response contains freshness info | | PUT | Creates or replace a resource | Yes | No | No | | PATCH | Partially updates a resource | No | No | Yes if response contains freshness info | | DELETE | Deletes a resource | Yes | No | No | *Can be called many times without different outcomes. HTTP is an application layer protocol relying on lower-level protocols such as **TCP** and **UDP**. #### Source(s) and further reading: HTTP * [What is HTTP?](https://www.nginx.com/resources/glossary/http/) * [Difference between HTTP and TCP](https://www.quora.com/What-is-the-difference-between-HTTP-protocol-and-TCP-protocol) * [Difference between PUT and PATCH](https://laracasts.com/discuss/channels/general-discussion/whats-the-differences-between-put-and-patch?page=1) ### Transmission control protocol (TCP)


Source: How to make a multiplayer game

TCP is a connection-oriented protocol over an [IP network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_Protocol). Connection is established and terminated using a [handshake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handshaking). All packets sent are guaranteed to reach the destination in the original order and without corruption through: * Sequence numbers and [checksum fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transmission_Control_Protocol#Checksum_computation) for each packet * [Acknowledgement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acknowledgement_(data_networks)) packets and automatic retransmission If the sender does not receive a correct response, it will resend the packets. If there are multiple timeouts, the connection is dropped. TCP also implements [flow control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flow_control_(data)) and [congestion control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_congestion#Congestion_control). These guarantees cause delays and generally result in less efficient transmission than UDP. To ensure high throughput, web servers can keep a large number of TCP connections open, resulting in high memory usage. It can be expensive to have a large number of open connections between web server threads and say, a [memcached](https://memcached.org/) server. [Connection pooling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connection_pool) can help in addition to switching to UDP where applicable. TCP is useful for applications that require high reliability but are less time critical. Some examples include web servers, database info, SMTP, FTP, and SSH. Use TCP over UDP when: * You need all of the data to arrive intact * You want to automatically make a best estimate use of the network throughput ### User datagram protocol (UDP)


Source: How to make a multiplayer game

UDP is connectionless. Datagrams (analogous to packets) are guaranteed only at the datagram level. Datagrams might reach their destination out of order or not at all. UDP does not support congestion control. Without the guarantees that TCP support, UDP is generally more efficient. UDP can broadcast, sending datagrams to all devices on the subnet. This is useful with [DHCP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_Host_Configuration_Protocol) because the client has not yet received an IP address, thus preventing a way for TCP to stream without the IP address. UDP is less reliable but works well in real time use cases such as VoIP, video chat, streaming, and realtime multiplayer games. Use UDP over TCP when: * You need the lowest latency * Late data is worse than loss of data * You want to implement your own error correction #### Source(s) and further reading: TCP and UDP * [Networking for game programming](https://gafferongames.com/post/udp_vs_tcp/) * [Key differences between TCP and UDP protocols](http://www.cyberciti.biz/faq/key-differences-between-tcp-and-udp-protocols/) * [Difference between TCP and UDP](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/5970383/difference-between-tcp-and-udp) * [Transmission control protocol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transmission_Control_Protocol) * [User datagram protocol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User_Datagram_Protocol) * [Scaling memcache at Facebook](http://www.cs.bu.edu/~jappavoo/jappavoo.github.com/451/papers/memcache-fb.pdf) ### Remote procedure call (RPC)


Source: Crack the system design interview

In an RPC, a client causes a procedure to execute on a different address space, usually a remote server. The procedure is coded as if it were a local procedure call, abstracting away the details of how to communicate with the server from the client program. Remote calls are usually slower and less reliable than local calls so it is helpful to distinguish RPC calls from local calls. Popular RPC frameworks include [Protobuf](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/), [Thrift](https://thrift.apache.org/), and [Avro](https://avro.apache.org/docs/current/). RPC is a request-response protocol: * **Client program** - Calls the client stub procedure. The parameters are pushed onto the stack like a local procedure call. * **Client stub procedure** - Marshals (packs) procedure id and arguments into a request message. * **Client communication module** - OS sends the message from the client to the server. * **Server communication module** - OS passes the incoming packets to the server stub procedure. * **Server stub procedure** - Unmarshalls the results, calls the server procedure matching the procedure id and passes the given arguments. * The server response repeats the steps above in reverse order. Sample RPC calls: ``` GET /someoperation?data=anId POST /anotheroperation { "data":"anId"; "anotherdata": "another value" } ``` RPC is focused on exposing behaviors. RPCs are often used for performance reasons with internal communications, as you can hand-craft native calls to better fit your use cases. Choose a native library (aka SDK) when: * You know your target platform. * You want to control how your "logic" is accessed. * You want to control how error control happens off your library. * Performance and end user experience is your primary concern. HTTP APIs following **REST** tend to be used more often for public APIs. #### Disadvantage(s): RPC * RPC clients become tightly coupled to the service implementation. * A new API must be defined for every new operation or use case. * It can be difficult to debug RPC. * You might not be able to leverage existing technologies out of the box. For example, it might require additional effort to ensure [RPC calls are properly cached](https://web.archive.org/web/20170608193645/http://etherealbits.com/2012/12/debunking-the-myths-of-rpc-rest/) on caching servers such as [Squid](http://www.squid-cache.org/). ### Representational state transfer (REST) REST is an architectural style enforcing a client/server model where the client acts on a set of resources managed by the server. The server provides a representation of resources and actions that can either manipulate or get a new representation of resources. All communication must be stateless and cacheable. There are four qualities of a RESTful interface: * **Identify resources (URI in HTTP)** - use the same URI regardless of any operation. * **Change with representations (Verbs in HTTP)** - use verbs, headers, and body. * **Self-descriptive error message (status response in HTTP)** - Use status codes, don't reinvent the wheel. * **[HATEOAS](http://restcookbook.com/Basics/hateoas/) (HTML interface for HTTP)** - your web service should be fully accessible in a browser. Sample REST calls: ``` GET /someresources/anId PUT /someresources/anId {"anotherdata": "another value"} ``` REST is focused on exposing data. It minimizes the coupling between client/server and is often used for public HTTP APIs. REST uses a more generic and uniform method of exposing resources through URIs, [representation through headers](https://github.com/for-GET/know-your-http-well/blob/master/headers.md), and actions through verbs such as GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, and PATCH. Being stateless, REST is great for horizontal scaling and partitioning. #### Disadvantage(s): REST * With REST being focused on exposing data, it might not be a good fit if resources are not naturally organized or accessed in a simple hierarchy. For example, returning all updated records from the past hour matching a particular set of events is not easily expressed as a path. With REST, it is likely to be implemented with a combination of URI path, query parameters, and possibly the request body. * REST typically relies on a few verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, and PATCH) which sometimes doesn't fit your use case. For example, moving expired documents to the archive folder might not cleanly fit within these verbs. * Fetching complicated resources with nested hierarchies requires multiple round trips between the client and server to render single views, e.g. fetching content of a blog entry and the comments on that entry. For mobile applications operating in variable network conditions, these multiple roundtrips are highly undesirable. * Over time, more fields might be added to an API response and older clients will receive all new data fields, even those that they do not need, as a result, it bloats the payload size and leads to larger latencies. ### RPC and REST calls comparison | Operation | RPC | REST | |---|---|---| | Signup | **POST** /signup | **POST** /persons | | Resign | **POST** /resign
{
"personid": "1234"
} | **DELETE** /persons/1234 | | Read a person | **GET** /readPerson?personid=1234 | **GET** /persons/1234 | | Read a person’s items list | **GET** /readUsersItemsList?personid=1234 | **GET** /persons/1234/items | | Add an item to a person’s items | **POST** /addItemToUsersItemsList
{
"personid": "1234";
"itemid": "456"
} | **POST** /persons/1234/items
{
"itemid": "456"
} | | Update an item | **POST** /modifyItem
{
"itemid": "456";
"key": "value"
} | **PUT** /items/456
{
"key": "value"
} | | Delete an item | **POST** /removeItem

"itemid": "456"
} | **DELETE** /items/456 |

#### Source(s) and further reading: REST and RPC * [Do you really know why you prefer REST over RPC](https://apihandyman.io/do-you-really-know-why-you-prefer-rest-over-rpc/) * [When are RPC-ish approaches more appropriate than REST?](http://programmers.stackexchange.com/a/181186) * [REST vs JSON-RPC](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/15056878/rest-vs-json-rpc) * [Debunking the myths of RPC and REST](https://web.archive.org/web/20170608193645/http://etherealbits.com/2012/12/debunking-the-myths-of-rpc-rest/) * [What are the drawbacks of using REST](https://www.quora.com/What-are-the-drawbacks-of-using-RESTful-APIs) * [Crack the system design interview](http://www.puncsky.com/blog/2016-02-13-crack-the-system-design-interview) * [Thrift](https://code.facebook.com/posts/1468950976659943/) * [Why REST for internal use and not RPC](http://arstechnica.com/civis/viewtopic.php?t=1190508)
explanation.how_it_works_internally: Network communication follows a layered model. Each layer adds its own header and handles a specific concern: physical transmission (L1-L2), addressing and routing (L3 IP), reliable delivery (L4 TCP/UDP), and application semantics (L7 HTTP/gRPC). When you type a URL, your request traverses all these layers down on the client, crosses the network, and traverses up on the server.

limitations: gRPC Debugging: Because Protobuf is binary, you cannot just use `curl` or browser dev tools easily to inspect payloads. You need specific tooling like `grpcurl` or BloomRPC.

WebSocket Scaling: Unlike stateless REST requests, WebSockets hold an open file descriptor on the server. To scale 1M concurrent users, you need dedicated connection handling servers and a Pub/Sub backplane (like Redis or Kafka) to route messages across instances.
HTTP/3 (QUIC) Adoption: While excellent for mobile networks (handles packet loss better than TCP), many enterprise firewalls heavily throttle or block UDP traffic, forcing fallbacks to HTTP/2.
common_mistakes: Choosing gRPC for a public-facing API without realizing browsers need a translation proxy (gRPC-Web).
Overusing WebSockets for simple request-response flows where long-polling or Server-Sent Events (SSE) would be drastically simpler.
Ignoring TLS handshake overhead in low-latency internal microservices (often internal microservices use plain HTTP/2 or mutual TLS depending on zero-trust policies).

children.title: DNS — Domain Name System
children.summary: How domain names are resolved to IP addresses — the hierarchical resolution process, record types, and DNS-based tricks for system design.

explanation.overview: DNS is the internet's phone book — it translates human-readable domain names (google.com) to IP addresses (142.250.80.46). Every HTTP request begins with a DNS lookup.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: RESOLUTION CHAIN (iterative): (1) Browser checks its local DNS cache. (2) If miss, OS resolver checks /etc/hosts then OS DNS cache. (3) If miss, query the configured DNS resolver (ISP or public like 8.8.8.8). (4) Resolver queries Root nameserver (13 clusters worldwide, anycast) → gets referral to .com TLD nameserver. (5) Resolver queries .com TLD nameserver → gets referral to google.com's authoritative nameserver (ns1.google.com). (6) Resolver queries authoritative nameserver → gets the A record (IP address). (7) Resolver caches the result (respects TTL) and returns to client. Total time: 50-200ms for uncached lookup, <1ms for cached. RECORD TYPES: A (IPv4 address), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias to another domain), MX (mail server), NS (nameserver), TXT (text — used for SPF, DKIM, domain verification), SRV (service discovery — host + port). TTL (Time To Live): how long resolvers cache the record. Low TTL (60s) = fast failover but more DNS queries. High TTL (86400s = 1 day) = fewer queries but slow failover.

key_concepts.definition: INTERNAL: DNS-based load balancing: return multiple A records (round-robin). Route 53 weighted routing: 70% traffic to region A, 30% to region B. Latency-based routing: resolve to the closest datacenter. Health checks: automatically remove unhealthy IPs from DNS responses. GeoDNS: resolve to different IPs based on client's geographic location (Cloudflare, Route 53). EDGE CASE: DNS caching means changes take time to propagate. During a migration, set TTL to 60s days before, then switch IPs, then raise TTL back. Some clients ignore TTL (especially Java's default DNS cache timeout of infinity — override with networkaddress.cache.ttl=30).

Multiple servers share the same IP address. BGP routing sends each client to the nearest server. Used by CDNs (Cloudflare has 300+ PoPs, all sharing the same anycast IP) and DNS root servers (13 addresses but hundreds of physical servers).

examples.title: Facebook 2021 Global Outage Case Study (BGP & DNS)
examples.description: A catastrophic failure demonstrating what happens when DNS and BGP routing fail simultaneously at a global scale.
examples.code:
What Happened:
During a routine maintenance job, Facebook engineers issued a command to assess global backbone capacity. A bug in the audit tool caused it to inadvertently take down all connections in the backbone network.

The Cascade:
Because the backbone went down, Facebook's DNS servers (which announce their IP addresses via BGP - Border Gateway Protocol) suddenly stopped announcing their routes to the global internet. To the rest of the world, Facebook's IP addresses effectively ceased to exist.

The Catch-22:
Engineers could not fix the issue remotely because the internal secure management network relied on the very DNS that was down. They had to physically travel to data centers, log into physical routers, and manually override the configurations.

Takeaway for Interviews:
Always separate the Control Plane (management tools) from the Data Plane (user traffic). If your management tools rely on the same network they manage, a failure locks you out.

children.title: TCP vs UDP — Transport Layer
children.summary: TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery with connection management. UDP provides fast, unreliable delivery with no overhead.

key_concepts.definition: Connection-oriented, reliable, ordered byte stream. HOW IT WORKS INTERNALLY: (1) Three-way handshake to establish connection: Client → SYN → Server. Server → SYN-ACK → Client. Client → ACK → Server. Connection established. Takes 1 RTT (~0.5ms same DC, ~150ms cross-continent). (2) Data transfer: sender transmits segments, receiver ACKs each. Lost segments are retransmitted. Segments are reassembled in order using sequence numbers. (3) Flow Control: receiver advertises a 'window size' — how many bytes it can buffer. Sender doesn't send more than the window. Prevents fast sender from overwhelming slow receiver. (4) Congestion Control: sender starts with a small window (slow start), doubles it each RTT until packet loss is detected, then reduces window. Algorithms: CUBIC (Linux default), BBR (Google — better for long-distance, high-bandwidth links). IMPLICATION: TCP is slower to start (handshake + slow start) but guarantees delivery. Ideal for: HTTP, database connections, file transfers, anything where data integrity matters.

Connectionless, unreliable, no ordering, no flow control. Sends datagrams independently — no handshake, no ACK, no retransmission. If a packet is lost, the application never knows (unless it implements its own reliability). ADVANTAGES: no handshake overhead (0 RTT), lower latency (no waiting for ACKs), supports multicast/broadcast. USE CASES: DNS queries (small, single request-response), video/audio streaming (losing a frame is better than delaying the stream — reconstruct or skip), online gaming (character positions — stale data is worse than missing data), IoT sensor data (high volume, small payloads, loss-tolerant). QUIC: Google's protocol that runs on UDP but adds connection establishment (1-RTT or 0-RTT with session resumption), reliability, multiplexing (no head-of-line blocking), and encryption (TLS 1.3 built-in). HTTP/3 uses QUIC. Why not just fix TCP? TCP is implemented in the OS kernel — updating TCP across billions of devices takes decades. QUIC runs in userspace and can be updated with application deployments.

children.title: HTTP / HTTPS — Application Layer
children.summary: Evolution from HTTP/1.0 to HTTP/3, TLS handshake internals, and keep-alive connection management.

key_concepts.definition: HTTP/1.0: new TCP connection per request (expensive — handshake on every request). HTTP/1.1 (1997): persistent connections (Connection: keep-alive, default ON). Multiple requests reuse the same TCP connection. But requests are serialized — head-of-line blocking: the second request waits for the first response. WORKAROUND: browsers open 6-8 parallel TCP connections per domain. TRICKS: domain sharding (serve images from img1.example.com, img2.example.com to get 6 connections per subdomain).

Single TCP connection per domain, multiplexed streams. Multiple requests and responses sent simultaneously over one connection as interleaved binary frames. Each request gets a stream ID — frames are reassembled by stream ID. Features: header compression (HPACK — maintains a dynamic table of previously sent headers, sends only deltas), server push (server proactively sends CSS/JS before client requests them), stream prioritization. LIMITATION: still runs on TCP, so packet loss at TCP layer blocks ALL streams (TCP-level head-of-line blocking).

Runs on QUIC (UDP-based), eliminating TCP head-of-line blocking. Each stream is independent — packet loss on one stream doesn't block others. 0-RTT connection resumption for repeat visitors. Built-in TLS 1.3 encryption. Connection migration — if your phone switches from WiFi to cellular, the connection survives (identified by connection ID, not IP+port).

TLS 1.3 (current standard): 1-RTT handshake. (1) Client Hello: supported cipher suites + key share (Diffie-Hellman public key). (2) Server Hello: chosen cipher suite + key share + certificate + Finished. (3) Client verifies certificate against trusted CAs, derives shared secret from key exchange, sends Finished. Full-duplex encrypted communication begins. TLS 1.2 was 2-RTT (separate key exchange step). TLS 1.3 combines key exchange and hello, saving one RTT. 0-RTT (session resumption): if client has connected before, it caches a pre-shared key (PSK) and sends encrypted data in the first packet. Risk: 0-RTT data can be replayed by an attacker — only use for idempotent requests (GET, not POST).

children.title: API Paradigms — REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL
children.summary: Three API paradigms — when to use each, internal mechanics, and trade-offs for system design.

key_concepts.definition: The most common API style. Resources identified by URLs (GET /users/123, POST /orders). Uses HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) and status codes (200 OK, 201 Created, 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found, 429 Rate Limited, 500 Internal Error). Data format: JSON (human-readable, verbose) or rarely XML. PROS: simple, universally understood, cacheable (GET responses cached by CDN/browser), stateless, tooling everywhere (Postman, curl, OpenAPI/Swagger). CONS: over-fetching (GET /users/123 returns all fields even if you only need name and email), under-fetching (need user + their posts + their followers = 3 separate requests), no built-in streaming (need SSE or WebSocket separately). BEST PRACTICES: use nouns not verbs (/users not /getUsers), use plural nouns (/users not /user), use query params for filtering (/users?role=admin&sort=name), version your API (/api/v1/users), use HATEOAS links for discoverability, implement cursor-based pagination (not offset), return proper HTTP status codes. USE WHEN: public APIs, CRUD applications, any client-facing API where simplicity and cacheability matter.

Binary protocol using Protocol Buffers (protobuf) for serialization, running on HTTP/2. Instead of resource-based URLs, you define services and methods in a .proto file: service UserService { rpc GetUser(GetUserRequest) returns (User); }. Protoc compiler generates client and server stubs in 10+ languages. DATA FORMAT: protobuf — binary encoding, 3-10× smaller than JSON, 10-100× faster to serialize/deserialize. Field identified by number (not name) — more compact, backward compatible (add fields with new numbers). STREAMING: gRPC supports 4 modes — unary (request → response), server streaming (1 request → N responses), client streaming (N requests → 1 response), bidirectional streaming (N → N). WHY SMALLER: JSON '{"name":"Alice","age":30}' = 27 bytes. Protobuf equivalent ≈ 9 bytes (field numbers + varint encoding). PROS: fastest serialization, strongly typed (protobuf schema = contract), auto-generated code, HTTP/2 multiplexing, native streaming. CONS: not human-readable (binary), harder to debug (need grpcurl or Bloom), not cacheable by CDN (binary + post-like), browser support limited (needs grpc-web proxy). USE WHEN: internal microservice communication where latency matters, polyglot environments (need Java, Python, Go clients), streaming use cases (live data feeds, video metadata).

Query language for APIs — client specifies exactly which fields it needs. Single endpoint (POST /graphql). Client sends: { user(id: 123) { name email posts { title } } } → server returns exactly those fields, nothing more. SOLVES: over-fetching (only get requested fields) and under-fetching (nested queries return related data in one request). INTERNAL: server defines a schema (type User { name: String!, email: String!, posts: [Post!]! }). Each field has a resolver function that fetches data. The GraphQL engine traverses the query, calls resolvers, and assembles the response. PROS: flexible queries (mobile gets fewer fields, web gets more), self-documenting (schema introspection), single round trip for complex data. CONS: N+1 query problem (naive resolvers — user → 20 posts → 20 author lookups = 21 DB queries. FIX: DataLoader batching), complex caching (no URL-based caching since all queries go to same endpoint — use persisted queries or Apollo cache), security concern (malicious deep/complex queries can DDoS — use query depth limiting, query cost analysis, and timeout). USE WHEN: mobile apps (minimize data transfer), complex client needs (dashboards pulling data from multiple services), rapid frontend iteration (frontend team can change data shape without backend changes).

Full-duplex, persistent connection between client and server over a single TCP connection. After an HTTP upgrade handshake (client sends Upgrade: websocket header, server responds 101 Switching Protocols), the connection stays open and both sides can send messages at any time. NO request-response pattern — bidirectional push. INTERNAL: after handshake, data is sent in frames (text or binary). Frames are lightweight — 2-14 bytes of header per message vs HTTP's hundreds of bytes of headers per request. Server can push to client without client requesting (unlike HTTP). HEARTBEAT: client and server exchange ping/pong frames to detect disconnections (typically every 30-60 seconds). SCALING CHALLENGE: each WebSocket connection is stateful and persistent. One server can hold ~10K-50K connections (limited by file descriptors and memory). For 10M concurrent users: need 200-1000 WebSocket servers. ROUTING: if User A wants to send a message to User B, and they're on different servers, you need a Pub/Sub layer (Redis Pub/Sub, Kafka) to route between servers. USE WHEN: chat (WhatsApp, Slack), live collaboration (Google Docs), real-time gaming, live dashboards, live sports scores.

Unidirectional server → client push over HTTP. Client opens a long-lived HTTP connection (Content-Type: text/event-stream), and the server sends events as they occur. Unlike WebSocket, SSE is HTTP-based — works with existing infrastructure (proxies, CDN, auth). SIMPLER than WebSocket but one-way only. Client can't send through the SSE connection (uses regular HTTP for sending). Auto-reconnect built into the browser API (EventSource). USE WHEN: live notifications, feed updates, stock tickers — any scenario where only the server pushes data.

examples.title: WebSocket Scaling Backplane (Python / FastAPI)
examples.description: When placing FastAPI WebSockets behind a load balancer, you must use a backplane like Redis Pub/Sub to broadcast messages across all active pods/workers.
examples.code:
# Python FastAPI with Redis Pub/Sub Broadcasting
@app.websocket("/ws/{client_id}")
async def websocket_endpoint(websocket: WebSocket, client_id: str):
    await websocket.accept()
    pubsub = redis.pubsub()
    await pubsub.subscribe("global_chat")
    
    async def reader(ws: WebSocket):
        async for message in pubsub.listen():
            if message["type"] == "message":
                await ws.send_text(message["data"])
                
    # Run reader task concurrently
    asyncio.create_task(reader(websocket))
    
    try:
        while True:
            data = await websocket.receive_text()
            # Broadcast to all pods via Redis
            await redis.publish("global_chat", f"{client_id}: {data}")
    except WebSocketDisconnect:
        await pubsub.unsubscribe("global_chat")

cons: gRPC: not human-readable, needs proxy for browser
tradeoffs.when_to_use: REST for external/public APIs. gRPC for internal service-to-service. GraphQL for complex client-driven queries. WebSocket for real-time bidirectional. SSE for server-push only.
tradeoffs.when_to_avoid: REST for real-time. gRPC for browser-facing. GraphQL for simple CRUD. WebSocket for request-response.

children.title: Networking & API Choice Decision Matrices
children.summary: A rubric-based checklist to justify API paradigm choices during interviews.

explanation.overview: When the interviewer asks 'Why REST instead of gRPC?' or 'Why WebSockets?', use these decision matrices.

key_concepts.definition: Does the client team and server team need a strictly enforced, compile-time contract? If yes, pick gRPC or GraphQL over plain REST.
Is the client a web browser? If yes, native gRPC is impossible without gRPC-Web proxy. REST or GraphQL are much better choices.

examples.title: Decision Matrix: API Paradigms
examples.description: How FAANG engineers confidently select API protocols.
examples.code:
REQUIREMENT                          | REST           | gRPC             | GraphQL          | WebSocket / SSE
-------------------------------------|----------------|------------------|------------------|--------------------
Contract Strictly Enforced           | No (Swagger)   | Yes (.proto)     | Yes (Schema)     | No
Payload Size (Bandwidth)             | Heavy (JSON)   | Light (Binary)   | Med (JSON)       | Light (Frames)
Browser Native Support               | Excellent      | Poor (needs proxy)| Excellent      | Excellent
Internal Microservice-to-Microservice| Good           | Excellent        | Poor             | Poor
Real-Time Bidirectional Data         | Poor (Polling) | Good (Streams)   | Subscriptions    | Excellent
Mitigates Over/Under-Fetching        | No             | No               | Excellent        | N/A
